chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Washsha', from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
In the book of Ali (peace be upon him): 'When the eye twitches, or the foot kicks, or the tail moves, eat from it, for its time of slaughter (zakah) has been reached.'

key_terms.تَحَرَّكَ الذَّنَبُ: The movement of the tail, a sign of life.
key_terms.ذَكَاتُهُ: The time or moment of permissible slaughter; here used to indicate the animal is alive and valid for consumption.
key_terms.رَكَضَتِ الرِّجْلُ: The kicking of the foot, a sign of life.
key_terms.طَرَفَتِ الْعَيْنُ: The twitching or blinking of the eye, a sign of life.
key_terms.فِي كِتَابِ عَلِيٍّ: In the book of Ali, referring to a recorded narration or legal text attributed to Imam Ali.

ai.seo_question: What are the signs that an animal is halal to eat without ritual slaughter according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Ali (peace be upon him), recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, elucidates the concept of *istihlak al-ruh* (cessation of life) for animals that do not undergo formal ritual slaughter (*dhabihah*). It establishes that natural physiological signs—such as eye twitching, foot kicking, or tail movement—serve as valid indicators that the animal has reached the permissible state for consumption, thereby simplifying the dietary laws for creatures like hares. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on observable biological markers of life and death in determining halal status.
